title: Find water outside
summary: Water runs downhill: check low ground, the foot of cliffs and dry stream beds.

list: Water runs downhill. Check valley bottoms and other low ground, the foot of cliffs or rocks, and dry stream beds; dig on the outside of bends.

blocks.cap: Dig on the outside of a bend in a dry stream bed. If you hit wet sand, dig down into it and let water seep in.

list: Signs of water nearby: lush green vegetation, swarming insects, game trails that meet in a V, and birds flying in the early morning or late afternoon, which may show the direction to water.
Catch rain on a tarp, poncho or large leaves.
Before sunrise, tie absorbent cloth around your ankles, walk through tall grass, and wring out the dew.
Tie a clear plastic bag over a leafy branch of a non-poisonous plant in full sun and seal it. Water collects in the bag as the leaves breathe.

blocks.cap: A transpiration bag. Collect the water before sundown. The same branch can be used for 3 to 5 days. The water tastes like the plant smells.

list: Never drink seawater or urine.
Skip lake or pond water that is strongly colored, looks like paint or has floating scum: it may be a harmful algal bloom, and treating it yourself does not make it safe (see Make water safe).
Treat all wild water, rain included, before drinking (see Make water safe).

blocks.p: Rain that runs off a roof picks up dirt, germs and chemicals: bird droppings, and asbestos, lead or copper from roofing, gutters and pipes. Rain after several dry days is the most likely to be dirty (CDC).

list: Let the first rain of each storm run off before you collect: that first flow carries the most dirt, germs and chemicals (CDC). Virginia Cooperative Extension suggests diverting 10 to 50 gallons for every 1,000 sq ft of roof (38 to 190 L for every 93 m²).
Water from wood, asphalt or tar shingle roofs may only be fit for watering plants (Virginia Cooperative Extension).
Screen where the water goes into a barrel, to keep out bugs and debris, or empty open barrels at least every 10 days so mosquitoes can’t breed in them (CDC).

blocks.warn: FEMA and Lake Champlain Sea Grant say not to drink collected rainwater. CDC says rainwater is not necessarily safe to drink without first removing germs and chemicals. Use roof water for washing, cleaning and flushing. Drink it only if you have nothing safer, and then filter it and boil or disinfect it. Boiling does not remove metals from the roof.

blocks.p: Don’t eat snow or ice: it lowers your body temperature (National Weather Service). Melt it, then treat it like any other wild water.

Rain, streams, rivers and other moving water, ponds, lakes and natural springs can all be made safe by treatment (CDC, FEMA). Rivers, streams and lakes might carry livestock waste, human sewage and chemicals (CDC).
Springs are fed by shallow groundwater and are easily contaminated. Most springs used for drinking need constant disinfection (Penn State Extension). Treat spring water like any other.
Wells can be contaminated by flooding (CDC).

list: Choose moving water over still water: faster water usually carries fewer harmful germs (Army ATP 3-50.21). FEMA lists streams, rivers and other moving water as sources.
Don’t take water from puddles and other natural dips in the ground: it is stagnant and often heavily contaminated (Army ATP 3-50.21).
Avoid water with floating material, an odor or a dark color (FEMA).
Water near towns, farms and camps is the most likely to carry human and animal waste (Army ATP 3-50.21, CDC).
Pick the clearest water you can. Cloudy water needs a double dose of bleach, and UV light and sunlight don’t work well in it (CDC).

blocks.p: Harmful algal blooms in New York look like pea soup, spilled green paint, long green streaks or scattered green dots, or turn the water blue-green or white (NYS DEC). They grow in warm, shallow, still, nutrient-rich water that gets a lot of sun (NYS Department of Health), and NYS DEC gets the most reports in August and September.

blocks.warn: Keep people, pets and livestock out of water that is discolored or has scum on it (NYS DEC). Filtering, chlorine or UV light at home may still not protect you from the toxins (NYS Department of Health). Showering, bathing or washing in bloom water also exposes you (NYS Department of Health).

blocks.p: Flood water: don’t drink it (FEMA). It can carry human and livestock waste, household, medical and industrial hazardous waste, and chemicals from containers the flood moved (CDC). Wash your hands with soap and clean water after touching it, and keep open wounds out of it (CDC).

Road salt can raise the sodium and chloride in water, which matters for anyone on a low-sodium diet or with high blood pressure or heart, kidney or liver disease (NYS Department of Health). Boiling and disinfecting leave salt in (EPA); a reverse osmosis filter (CDC, NYS Department of Health) or distillation (FEMA) takes it out.

Fuel and chemicals: avoid water that may carry toxins (Army ATP 3-50.21), such as water near old factories, mines, dumps or spills, or water that smells of fuel or chemicals. Boiling and disinfecting can’t make it safe (CDC): find another source.

list: Carry water in clean containers with tight lids (CDC).
Keep the containers you fill with untreated water apart from your drinking-water containers, and mark them.
If the water is cloudy or muddy, let it stand so the dirt settles, then pour off the clear water (CDC, WHO). The Army says several hours; WHO says storing it for 2 days reduces contamination further.
Then filter it through a clean cloth, paper towel or coffee filter and treat it (CDC, EPA).
